content: The University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics (UIHC) is a 762-bed public teaching hospital and a Level 1 trauma center affiliated with the University of Iowa. It is part of the University of Iowa Health Care system, which is a collaboration between the University of Iowa Roy J. and Lucille A. Carver College of Medicine and the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics. The hospital is located in Iowa City, Iowa, at the intersection of Melrose Avenue and Hawkins Drive, near Kinnick Stadium. During televised Hawkeye football games, the hospital is often visible in the background. UIHC is one of three hospitals in Iowa City, alongside Mercy Hospital Iowa City and the Iowa City VA Medical Center. The hospital employs over 7,100 individuals and is governed by the Iowa Board of Regents. It is the only comprehensive, tertiary-level medical center in Iowa and is considered the state’s premier medical facility. Patients from across the state are frequently referred to UIHC for the treatment of serious or complex illnesses and injuries. The University of Iowa began providing medical services in 1873 when its medical department partnered with the Sisters of Mercy to operate a small hospital in the community. Dr. Washington Freeman Peck, a physician from Davenport, Iowa, and other physicians raised $5,000 to renovate a vacant school building, known as Mechanics Academy, into a 20-bed hospital. This facility included two open wards for men and women, four private rooms, and a surgical amphitheater. Dr. Peck persuaded the Mother Superior of the Davenport-based Sisters of Mercy to send nuns to Iowa City to assist in patient care. This arrangement lasted until 1885, when the Sisters moved to a nearby vacant mission and opened Mercy Hospital a year later. As the University outgrew its original facility, the need for a new hospital became evident. In 1896, the state of Iowa approved the necessary appropriations, and a 65-bed hospital was constructed in 1898 at the site where Seashore Hall now stands. This facility was state-of-the-art for its time, featuring both electrical lighting and steam heating. It also included a 200-seat amphitheater for instructional purposes. Following the passage of indigent care laws in 1928, patient admissions increased significantly. The current hospital was built in 1928 as a 735-bed facility, and at the time of its construction, it was one of the largest hospital buildings in the country. As of 2007, eight hospital specialties at UIHC were ranked among the top 50 in the nation by U.S. News & World Report. These specialties included Otolaryngology (ranked 2nd), Ophthalmology (6th), Orthopedics (16th), Neurology and Neurosurgery (18th), Urology (22nd), Kidney Disease (26th), Gynecology (32nd), and Digestive Disorders (40th). More than 150 UI physicians have been recognized as “Best Doctors in America” by their peers. UIHC has also been designated as a Wellmark Center of Excellence in Bariatric Surgery and is one of fewer than 60 National Cancer Institute (NCI)-designated comprehensive cancer centers in the United States. It was the first hospital in Iowa to receive the Magnet Award for Nursing Excellence. Additionally, UIHC was the development site for buffered aspirin, later marketed by Bristol-Myers as Bufferin. It was the first hospital in the world to implant a multichannel cochlear implant, enabling deaf patients to hear sounds interpretable as speech, and the first to implant such a device in a congenitally deaf child. UIHC was also the first research center to discover the gene responsible for open-angle glaucoma. It pioneered the use of robotic surgery for the removal of adrenal carcinoma and adrenal masses in pediatric patients. Furthermore, it was the first hospital in the U.S. to perform digital breast tomosynthesis imaging, allowing physicians to examine the interior of the breast without the superimposition of other tissues. Several groundbreaking medical advances have been achieved at UIHC. In 1939, Dr. Elmer L. DeGowin and his team developed modern blood banking techniques, enabling the refrigeration, transportation, and use of banked blood. In 1971, the world’s first horizontal gastroplasty surgery for morbid obesity was performed at the hospital. In 1982, UIHC otolaryngologists were the first in the country to place a multichannel cochlear implant in a patient. More recently, in 2005, the Center of Excellence in Image-Guided Radiation Therapy, the world’s most advanced radiation oncology treatment center, was established at UIHC.
